bio.en: Mark Pincus is the founder of Zynga, the social-gaming pioneer behind FarmVille, and a serial consumer-internet entrepreneur and investor.
bio.zh: 马克·平卡斯（Mark Pincus）是 Zynga 的创始人，即《FarmVille》背后的社交游戏先驱，也是一位连续消费互联网创业者与投资人。

summary.en: Mark offers contrarian advice like "burn your resume" if you're truly ambitious, trusting your instincts (right ~95% of the time) over ideas (wrong ~75%). He warns against founders who stoically cling to losing ideas instead of reading market signals. The episode is a blunt, experienced take on spotting real product-market fit and avoiding self-deception.
summary.zh: 马克给出了反共识的建议：如果你真的有野心，就"烧掉你的简历"，并相信直觉（约 95% 正确）而非想法（约 75% 错误）。他警告那些固执地抱着失败想法、不去读取市场信号的创始人。本期以坦诚而老练的口吻，讲述了如何识别真正的产品-市场契合、避免自欺。

turns.en: It's almost a moral arbitrage. 因此，“验证、改进、创新”的核心理念就是要说：“让我们先把那些已被验证的方案排除在外。” 如果你想打造一款AI版的Snapchat或AI相机（我现在看到太多这类产品了），那没问题。但首先，你得先处理那些尚未创新之处——比如图标设计，或相机的工作机制。看看哪些方面在市场上已经做到极致，无论是苹果、Snapchat还是Instagram，都可以合法借鉴。只要能保持口味不变，我们就能区分出优秀的模仿品和劣质复制品，但首先要精通已有的验证方案。先在验证层面深耕，再去探索改进之处。

（00:08:32）而“改进”通常意味着我们找不到更优的方案。改进往往是微小的迭代和创新，比如10个现有用户中有9个会说“太棒了”的改进。（不是你，而是大众的共识）你认为好的改进，可能是我们眼中的“新”。在Words With Friends这款游戏中，我们借鉴了Scrabble，但如果只是Scrabble本身，凭什么能吸引1400万日活用户？肯定还有更出色的创新点。比如社交功能——用户的Facebook好友列表一键同步，让他们随时能组队玩游戏，这就是个创新点。

（00:09:46）至于“创新”，要找到能让用户下载尝试的新奇创意。Words With Friends的创新点在于社交属性——用户的好友列表与Facebook图谱无缝对接，随时能组队游戏。即便你觉得“这太明显了”，但未必所有人都认同，往往这种创新会失败。不过至少能吸引用户尝试。

（00:10:21）如果能正确践行“验证、改进、创新”策略，产品成功的概率会大大增加，避免走弯路。比如当我们假设新创意可能行不通时，就用不同方式验证。

（00:10:46）我觉得如果能正确实施“验证、改进、创新”策略，就像拥有一台时间机器。假如回到2003年的马克·扎克伯格，告诉他：“老兄，你根本不知道自己的直觉有多正确。其中一个想法未来会创造1.6万亿美元市值。”那他就领先同行一年了。我不会具体透露，但可以告诉你：“这里还有其他值得尝试的方向，能创造1.6万亿美元市值。顺便说一句，你的Tribes概念，后来演变成了Reddit的行业列表功能。”

我的成功几率。

And then add something new that nobody's tried before, that adds a little wrinkle. (00:12:41): And I think a little bit like you have a bunch of examples in the book, Slack and Threads. There's also like, if you think about the iPhone and the iPod, you don't think about them that way, but basically the iPod, there was a music player, they made it better and they added some new stuff and it-
turns.zh: 好的。这里内容太多了。所以让我来总结一下我对这个框架的看法，这个框架确实很棒。如果你真正思考一下所有成功的产品，以及其中有多少产品实际上遵循了这个框架——无论他们是否有意识地这样做——这真是令人惊叹的。我听到的步骤是，先验证已有的成功案例，接着优化现有产品，最后推出创新功能。（00:12:21）：先验证是指列出市场上已被证明有效的产品，以及人们对某个领域的喜爱之处。优化则意味着打造一款不仅更出色，而且能让10个人中有10个会说：“太棒了，我愿意换用它。它就是更好。” 然后加入一些前所未有的新元素，增添一些小惊喜。（00:12:41）：我认为书中有很多例子，比如Slack和Threads。再比如iPhone和iPod，你可能不会这么想，但基本上，iPod原本就是一款音乐播放器，他们对其进行了优化并添加了新功能——

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... was one of the best products in the world.
turns.zh: ……它是世界上最出色的产品之一。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: And I was there at the TED conference when this team from MIT was demoing their touchscreen. And they did it on a gigantic whiteboard and Steve Jobs was obsessed with it. They had a whiteboard and they had a table with it and I watched him and he spent the whole time there with this team obsessing over their touch. I don't know if that's the first time he saw it, but I know he was obsessed with it like, okay, there's his new idea is a touchscreen. It's only new idea. And I want to say proven gets so misused. And that what I've found over the years with founders is that they start to use Proven, Better, New to justify a wrong idea. And they're like, "Look, Mark, I'm doing proven. Proven is this game that was popular in the '90s. Proven is," and they pick something and it's to their own detriment, they're not using proven ... We have to be precise. We have to think at the pixel level of this experience. Proven is on this platform for this audience, for this experience. And you can look to what's been proven before as great sources of new ideas, but if it's not on this platform, it doesn't count as proven. (00:14:25): And yet the masters at this product craft do Proven, Better, New, whether they call it that or not, and they do it at such a beautiful level that nobody even thinks ... No one realizes what it's derivative of. And Slack was a great example because I think Slack might've just been proven and better and no new and that's even better. If you can have a successful product, and I don't want to sound anti-innovation, but people don't like change. So if you take a behavior they like, but you make it much more accessible or something much more fun about it, like in the case of Slack, people love that even more.
turns.zh: 我在TED大会上见过麻省理工学院的团队展示他们的触摸屏。他们在一个巨大的白板上演示，史蒂夫·乔布斯对此着迷不已。他们用白板和桌子展示，我观察到他整个时间都在和团队纠结于触摸屏的细节。我不知道这是他第一次看到触摸屏，但我知道他对此着迷极了。好吧，他的新想法就是触摸屏。这只是个新想法。我想“验证”这个词被滥用得太严重了。多年来我发现，很多创业者会用“验证、优化、创新”来为错误的想法辩护。比如他们会说：“看啊，马克，我在做验证。验证就是90年代流行的那个游戏。验证就是……”然后他们选个例子，但这对他们自己反而有害，他们并没有真正理解“验证”的含义……我们必须精确。我们必须在体验的微观层面思考。验证就是在现有平台、现有受众、现有体验中进行验证。你可以把之前已被验证的东西视为新想法的来源，但如果它不在现有平台上，就不算验证。（00:14:25）：然而，产品设计大师们无论是否称之为验证、优化、创新，都在践行这个框架，而且做得极为出色，以至于没人会察觉……没人意识到这源自何处。而Slack就是一个很好的例子，我认为Slack可能只是验证了现有产品，优化了现有功能，没有推出新元素，但这反而更棒。如果你能打造一款成功的产品——我不想显得反创新，但人们不喜欢改变。所以如果你取用他们喜欢的某种行为，但让它更易用、更有趣，比如Slack的情况，人们会更爱它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this thread of copying that comes through this framework that will turn a lot of people off. Talk about what you think people are missing and how you get over that hump of like this is actually the right approach in most cases.
turns.zh: 这个框架中存在模仿的倾向，这会让很多人望而却步。谈谈你认为人们忽略了什么，以及如何克服这种障碍，即在大多数情况下，这确实是正确的方法。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: In the Peter Thiel sense, it's almost a moral arbitrage because there's something in our gut as a product maker. You became a founder, an entrepreneur because you wanted to go be an innovator. So it can feel like a beat down that your path to innovation starts with copying other people's work. And we are taught in school, copying is cheating. So there's a lot of good reasons why we've built this kind of moral resistance to copying. (00:16:06): But that also makes that opportunity in some ways more available for people who have less ego involved. And I like to say, and I said this to my product makers at Zynga, if you're truly ambitious, burn your resume. And if you define your ambition in the eyes of your consumer, not your peers, you're not trying to win awards and respect from your peers, you're trying to win the hearts and minds of nurses in Indiana, like for Farmville, you're going to define innovation differently and you're not going to worry about whether ... You're going to take the best ideas wherever you can find them if they are in service of giving her an experience that she loves more. (00:16:57): So if all you did was copy, there's no reason for her to choose your product, right? But if you took something that she loves and you make it one inch better, she might love that more than if you showed her something she's never seen before and didn't wake up knowing that she wanted. And I think that the art of this is you do it in a way that she doesn't even realize it. (00:17:30): Because I think consumer taste also resists just a copy. I think that if movies, TV shows, books, if they feel too derivative and they're not adding something important and new, then it could go against our consumer taste. But the best product makers, and I love referencing someone like Craig Newmark and Craigslist, who took two years to add photos to Craigslist listings. And he lived in my neighborhood and he was friends with my dog, Zynga, more than he was friends with me. He was a little awkward socially and he connected more with the dog and I tried to be friends with him through the dog. (00:18:15): So he would sit and talk to me and he was working on ... I was like, "What are you working on?" He said, "I've been working for two years on adding photos to listings." I'm like, "What do you mean two years?" He's like, "Well, I really want to make sure that people like it and that the photos come up in the right ways." I don't know. I honestly don't even understand what he did for two years. But if you're driving across San Francisco to buy someone's couch, why isn't that better? In his mind, it was new. And I'm like, "That's a world-class product maker because what he gets is that his ..." (00:18:50): We feel this sense of ownership of products that we rely on every day and we're angry when they change. Even if they change for the better, we're angry because we go through life faster because of pattern recognition and we don't want to think about these things. And what if by adding photos to his listings, he moved where the text was and what if you rifle through listings and now the text is below the fold? And a junior product maker might make the whole thing a picture and not realize that what people liked most was being able to see the text real quick and they were trying to compare prices on the couch they already knew that ... I don't know.
turns.zh: 用彼得·泰尔的话来说，这几乎是一种道德上的权衡，因为作为产品制造商，我们内心深处总有这样的矛盾心理。你成为创始人、创业者，是因为你想成为创新者。所以，当你发现自己的创新之路始于模仿他人作品时，可能会感到挫败。毕竟，学校里教导我们，抄袭就是作弊。因此，我们对模仿行为天然存在道德抗拒。（00:16:06）但这也为那些不那么在意面子的人创造了更多机会。我常对Zynga的产品团队说：如果你足够有雄心，就烧掉你的简历吧。当你把消费者放在首位，而非迎合同行评判时，当你努力赢得印第安纳州护士的心，而非争取奖项和尊重时，当你愿意借鉴他人精华，只要能提升用户体验时，你对创新的定义就会截然不同。（00:16:57）所以，如果你只是照搬别人的成果，用户凭什么选择你的产品？但如果你能将用户喜爱的元素再提升一英寸，他们或许会比从未见过的新事物更爱它。我认为关键在于让用户在不知不觉中受益。（00:17:30）因为消费者本能地抗拒直白的模仿。电影、电视剧、书籍若缺乏创新元素，必将违背审美习惯。然而最优秀的产品经理——比如克雷格·纽马克和Craigslist——用了两年时间才在列表中添加照片。他住在我家附近，跟我的狗Zynga比跟我更熟。他社交能力欠佳，更能与狗狗建立联系。我试图通过狗狗和他成为朋友。（00:18:15）他会坐下来跟我聊天，谈论……我问：“你在做什么？” 他说：“我花了两年时间优化照片上传功能。” 我：“什么意思，花了两年？” 他说：“我必须确保用户体验流畅，照片展示效果自然。” 我实在不明白他为什么折腾两年。但如果在旧金山买沙发时，照片功能能让用户更直观选购，在他看来就是世界级创新。（00:18:50）我们对日常依赖的产品怀有归属感，当它们改版时会愤然不满。即便改进是良性的，我们也会不满，因为生活节奏加快，我们懒得深思熟虑。例如添加照片功能后，文本位置调整会让用户翻页查找信息。初级产品经理可能把整个界面都换成图片，却没意识到用户最需要的是快速查看文本信息，方便比较价格……我也说不清。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. As you're talking, I'm just thinking what are all the best products and are they all just kind of one word ... Are they copies and evolutions of existing products or how many are just completely brand new? And I'm looking around like the iPhone, there's phones before and they kind of took the elements of what was great, made them awesome. My Owala, I don't know, water bottle, there was water bottles that worked and then they added things to make it better. Chrome, I don't know. I'm just looking around. It's so interesting how once you start to think about it through this lens, most products are better versions of things that existed before. A. (00:20:04): Nd then I'm thinking about as a product team, what do you often do? You go, look at the competitors, look at all their flows, here's what they're doing, here's what's working, look at all these great ideas, and then you build on that. So I think it's easy to get turned off to this idea of the word copy, but as you think about it, this is mostly how products end up getting built anyway.
turns.zh:
是啊。你说话的时候，我一直在想，市面上那些优秀的产品都是什么？它们是不是都只用一个词来概括……它们是现有产品的复制品和改进版，还是完全全新的产品？比如iPhone之前也有手机，但苹果把那些优秀的元素整合起来，做得更出色。Owala水壶，我不知道，之前也有能用的水壶，但Owala在此基础上加了更多实用功能。Chrome浏览器也是如此。我只是在观察这一切。很有趣的是，一旦你从这个角度去思考，大多数产品都是对前人成果的改进版本。

A.（00:20:04）：然后我就在想，作为产品团队，你们通常会怎么做？你们会去研究竞争对手的产品流程，观察他们的设计思路，分析哪些地方效果显著，再从中汲取灵感进行改进。所以我觉得人们很容易对“抄袭”这个词反感，但仔细想想，产品最终形成的过程大多都是这样的。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Well, there's so much on this that we could literally spend the whole podcast on it, which I'd be fine with too, or do a whole episode just on this because so much comes up for me. On the one hand, I think about Nikita, who I think you've had on. And I love his story on TBH. It's a perfect example of he found something proven in someone else's product. That was my first company, Freeloader. What I found was in the Netscape browser and in the Internet Explorer browser, they had buried in there a feature of offline browsing. And my entire product was offline browsing. But they had it as this buried power user feature and I saw the genius in that for that moment because bandwidth was so slow that I was like, "Oh, we can make an entire product just around that one feature." Nikita saw his perfect product buried inside an Arabic only version of his product and he said, "Oh my God, they nailed it." So I think when we can see something that is proven already in someone else's product, but they have the wrong idea around it, that's gold. (00:21:50): And then to your question of is every product derivative? Is every product from Proven, Better, New? My answer is no. And I talked about this a little bit in the book and in my course, but the question is at the outset for all of us, which path do you want to be on? And I argue that if you go down this path of just innovate, start with a blank whiteboard, don't look at any other products, that is kind of Rovio getting to Angry Birds. They made 45 games. Every single game was totally different, not, as far as I could tell, learning from the previous failures or the market and their 45th shot on goal was Angry Birds and it was a hit and it was innovative. But the odds, that's wildcat drilling and do you want to have those odds? (00:22:45): Or do you want to do what OMGPOP did, which is very similar story but opposite path, which was OMGPOP created the hit game Draw Something and Zynga bought them. They were the number one game and app in the App Store for 60 days in 2012. But OMGPOP was on their last dollar. They had tried something totally innovative. No one ever seen or tried it before, it failed completely. And now they were ruthlessly, desperately in need of a hit and now they did Proven, Better, New perfectly. They said, "We're going to take this proven game and do everything about it as perfect students of what is already working and viral on mobile." And they perfectly copied our turn-based system from Words With Friends and they made a massive hit.
turns.zh:
好吧，这个话题实在太丰富了，我们可以整个播客都来探讨它——我倒也不介意，或者专门做一期节目来深入讨论，因为它让我有很多感触。一方面，我想到了尼基塔（Nikita），我记得你曾邀请过他。他在TBH上的故事太精彩了，简直是典型的从他人产品中发现可用素材的案例。这是我创办的首家公司Freeloader的灵感来源。我发现Netscape和Internet Explorer浏览器都隐藏了离线浏览功能，而我的整个产品就是围绕这一功能打造的。但他们把这项功能设计成深藏不露的高级用户功能，当时我立刻意识到其中的巧思——毕竟当时的网络带宽太慢，我当时就想：“哦，我们完全可以围绕这一功能打造整个产品。”尼基塔在自己的产品阿拉伯语版中发现了类似的功能，他惊呼：“天哪，他们真是深藏不露的高手。”所以，当我们能从他人已验证的产品中发现可用素材，却发现他们对此有误解时，这就是绝佳的机会。

（00:21:50）再回到你的问题：每个产品都是衍生品吗？每个产品都遵循“已验证、更优、创新”的路径吗？我的答案是否定的。我在书中和课程中都略微谈及这个问题，但核心问题是，我们每个人在起步时就该明确：你想走哪条路？我认为，如果你选择创新之路，从空白画布出发，不参考其他产品，那就是Rovio开发《愤怒的小鸟》的模式。他们开发了45款游戏，每款都截然不同，据我所知，没有从前期失败或市场反馈中吸取教训，直到第45次尝试才击中目标。但这种赌博式创新，你真想冒这个险吗？

（00:22:45）或者你想效仿OMGPOP的做法？这是一个相似但相反的例子。OMGPOP开发了热门游戏《画画猜词》，被Zynga收购。2012年，他们曾连续60天称霸App Store。但当时OMGPOP已是穷途末路，他们尝试过完全创新、前无古人的产品，结果彻底失败。如今他们迫切需要救命稻草，于是完美地实践了“已验证、更优、创新”策略。他们复制了我们《Words With Friends》的回合制玩法，最终大获成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hell yeah. I love this idea of moral arbitrage, that's such a ... Thinking about this-
turns.zh: 太棒了。我超爱这种道德套利的理念，这真是……想想这个——

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: It's very Peter Thiel-ian, you know?
turns.zh: 这太彼得·泰尔式思维了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So there's so many fun threads that kind of connect to all this. And you have all these amazing contrarian perspectives on how to build amazing products. One is be less ambitious. Talk about why that's a really good lens to actually build more ambitious products.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以有很多有趣的线索能串联起所有这些话题。你分享了这么多关于如何打造卓越产品的逆向观点，真是太棒了。其中一条就是降低野心。谈谈为什么这正是打造更具雄心的产品的绝佳视角。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: I'm in the middle of relearning that lesson myself right now. And I would say there's so many paradoxes in this and one that I've had to learn over and over again is if we're too ambitious at the outset and too ambitious and visionary about the product we want to build, then we will probably miss product market fit because we won't start at a small enough, humble enough place because it might ... Usually the starting point for these products is embarrassingly small. So many of these massive hit products or franchises started with such humble-
turns.zh: 眼下我自己也正处于重新领悟这一教训的过程中。我想说，这其中存在诸多悖论，其中一个我反复领教的教训是：如果我们一开始就过于雄心勃勃，对想打造的产品有着过高的期望和远大构想，那么很可能就会错失产品与市场的契合点，因为我们没有从足够小、足够谦逊的起点出发……通常这类产品的起点小得令人难为情。许多后来大获成功的产品或品牌，刚开始时都非常不起眼——

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Started with such humble non-ambitious places and The Facebook was just an app to check out girls and guys at Harvard. And the irony for me is I've found that my career has gone in these waves and maybe some of your other founders have had this experience too, that I've started in a very humble place of, "I just want to get to anything, any product market fit", had bigger success than I imagined I would have in my first two companies, Freeloader and Support.com. They both started with very small, humble premise. And then afterwards felt like now I can do anything. And I know Elon is the exception to the rule. Part of it is I think he can raise magical unlimited amounts of capital, which helps, but then he does not start in humble places at all. But for the rest of us mortals, I'd say that we tend to after success feel the need to do something bigger the next time. That's human instinct and we want to be more ambitious. (00:26:20): And so when I got to Tribe and I saw social networking and LinkedIn was just starting and I saw how big the opportunity was, I tried to do everything with Tribe. It was really ambitious and I didn't pick one use case. And there was multiple inside Tribe that worked. The tribes, the idea of these urban tribes worked. People loved it, but it was too ambitious and so we failed. And then I was so humbled and I was in this abyss we can talk about for so long and I was so just desperate to get out of that abyss that by the time I got to Zynga, I did something that was embarrassingly small. (00:27:03): I mean, to be 41, multi-time successful founder that could go do something important in the world and what did I do? I made a Facebook app like a poker game, not even a Facebook app, I mean a poker game. It was people thought I had no dignity. I mean people were like, "Mark, there's so much you could do in the world." But I'd say my ambition came down to a 1000 ft altitude, not a 100,000 ft. And that was the key to that being successful. And I see this with, it's just so hard. I see it with so many product founders and it almost gives a new founder an advantage over a multi-time successful founder because we have too much rope to hang ourselves. It's too easy to raise money and recruit teams against a big vision before we've gotten to product market fit, but the world doesn't care about your resume. That's the good news for everyone watching. Everyone has the same chance and in a lot of ways if you're in a more humble place, you have a better opportunity. So the paradox is the more ambitious you are that the more humble you should be in the smaller place you should be willing to start.
turns.zh: 起初，Facebook只是哈佛学生用来结交异性朋友的应用程序，而我创业之路的讽刺之处在于，我发现自己的职业生涯也经历了类似的起起落落。或许其他创业者也有过类似经历——我最初的创业历程始于一个非常低调的阶段，满脑子都是“只要能把产品推向市场就行”。然而，在创办Freeloader和Support.com这两家公司时，我取得了超出预期的成功。这两家公司最初的定位都非常低调。但随后，那种“我能无所不能”的膨胀感又接踵而至。当然，埃隆·马斯克是个例外——他能轻松募集到巨额资金，这确实有助于他突破常规。但对于我们这些普通人来说，成功往往会催生更大的野心。（00:26:20）当我创办Tribe时，社交网络领域正兴起，LinkedIn刚刚起步，我意识到其中的巨大机遇。当时我试图用Tribe平台做成一切事务，野心勃勃却没有专注于某个核心场景。虽然Tribe中的多个功能都行得通，但最终还是失败了。那段低谷时期让我倍感挫败，急于摆脱困境以至于转投Zynga时，做的却是一款尴尬的小游戏——一个Facebook应用程序，甚至都算不上真正的Facebook应用。人们觉得我太没出息，纷纷劝道："马克，你本可以改变世界的。"但我选择把野心缩减至千尺而非万里，这才是成功的关键。许多产品创始人都深有体会——成功越多的创业者越容易陷入自我膨胀的陷阱，在尚未找到产品市场契合点前就急于融资扩张团队。但现实不会因你的履历而放过任何人。对每位观众而言，关键在于机会均等。如果你能保持低调，恰恰拥有更佳的破局机会。正如马克所言，野心越大，越要从低处起步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of your insights along these lines is that this is your advantage as a startup is to be less ambitious because a Zuck needs to go really big because the revenue is already so high. Anything they take on needs to be many billion-dollar business opportunity. And as a startup, you don't need to do that. And this is how you end up discovering some of the biggest ideas in the end.
turns.zh: 您在这方面的洞察之一是，作为初创公司，您不必过于雄心勃勃，因为扎克伯格（Zuck）必须追求宏大目标，因为他的公司营收已经很高了。初创公司无需承受这种压力。正因如此，你们最终才能发现一些最伟大的创意。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Being willing to pursue these little threads when they're flaky, when they're not a business, when they're so much earlier, and so many of the successful companies today started there.
turns.zh: 当这些想法看似不切实际、尚未形成商业模式、处于早期阶段时，初创公司也要愿意去探索。如今许多成功的公司都是从这些微小的尝试起步的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that comes to mind when, because what's a company or two that started very unambitious?
turns.zh: 您能否举个例子？比如，有哪家初创公司是从低调起步、后来大获成功的？

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: I love the story of Bolt.new that really blew up last year. I loved it so much. I coldmailed the founder because I was just so impressed with-
turns.zh: 我很喜欢去年火爆的Bolt.new的故事。我对它的创始人印象深刻，甚至主动发邮件联系了他——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:29:14]?

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: ... Yeah. And they toiled an obscurity on something that they were into and then they open sourced it. I think they were barely able to keep going with commercial development. And then they had this realization one day of, "Wait a second, if we take these web stacks, this virtual machine that we've been making work on the web, but we actually add that to an AI coding copilot, we now have something that's better than what anybody else has." And I think that was just a great story that they were passionate about one thing and they stuck with it.
turns.zh: ……是的。他们埋头于自己热爱的事业，后来将其开源。当时商业化进程举步维艰。直到有一天，他们突然意识到：“等等，如果我们把这些网络技术栈，加上我们在网络上成功运行的虚拟机，再融入AI编程助手，就能打造出超越现有产品的创新。”我觉得这就是个绝佳案例——他们对某个领域充满热情，并坚持不懈地深耕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Eric was on the podcast. We talked about that.
turns.zh: 埃里克上过我们的播客，我们讨论过这个案例。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Oh, he was? I'm so impressed. In a lot of ways, Slack also was humbled. Stewart keeps trying to start game companies and those turn into unexpected bigger hit companies. We'll see what he does. And actually now has probably so much capital he could just keep doing a game company this time.
turns.zh: 哦，他上过吗？真是佩服。他在很多方面也曾低调行事，比如斯图尔特（Stewart）一直想创办游戏公司，但最终都意外发展成大热门。看看他接下来会怎么做。说实话，他现在手头资金充足，完全可以再试一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But I think to your point, he might try again to unhumble, go big.
turns.zh: 但我觉得他可能还是会再次挑战自我，追求更宏大的目标。

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: But each time, so he started a big idea for the mass-market MMO, which I've also loved, but really difficult. And they were humbled in that enough to say, "Okay, wait, there's this little teeny thing that our engineers use. Let's build a product around that." And it really takes a really attuned, curious, humble founder to call the ball on that. I mean, I can imagine, I guess I've been there how hard it is when you've got investors and team and everybody going in one direction and we have to express confidence as founders. Whether or not we have actual confidence inside, that's part of, I think, the dissonance of this. How do you express confidence? How do you stay in a place of intellectual honesty? How do we stay authentic and transparent and not rattle our team? (00:31:41): And I'm still learning. I err on the side of transparency and honesty and being authentic to a fault and I burn out people in that process and I did at Zynga and I have since because people will say, the negative critique I'm working with me is, "Oh, working for Mark is like third grade soccer and every Monday he comes in excited about a different idea." And they're not wrong. But where I can get better at this maybe is if we can build a culture with our team that says, "Okay, we are ambitious. We're so ambitious that we're not going to hold onto a B+. Even if we could get funding, even if it has some traction, we have a north star that we are not going to stop until we find product market fit against our north star and this isn't it and it's going to take courage on our part. And hey, let's look around the room. Is everyone ambitious enough to do this? Or do you want to peel off and go join someone else who's already a rocket ship?" That's a fair career choice for you to make. But I think that's to me the real founder mode is can you have the courage to tell your team and your investors that this isn't it?
turns.zh: 是啊，每次都是这样。他会为面向大众市场的MMO游戏构想宏大的蓝图，我也很欣赏这种雄心，但这确实难度极大。他们最终会虚心地意识到："好吧，先等等，我们工程师用的这个小工具挺有用的，不如围绕它打造一款产品。" 要想做到这点，就需要一位敏锐、好奇且谦逊的创始人来果断决策。我能想象那种情境——投资者、团队成员都一心想朝着某个方向前进，而作为创始人，你必须表现出自信。无论内心是否真的有信心，这都构成了认知上的冲突。该如何传递出自信？如何保持思想的诚实？又如何既真实透明又不致让团队动摇？（00:31:41）：我至今仍在学习中。我倾向于保持透明、诚实，力求真实到近乎偏执的程度，但这会让团队感到疲惫——我在Zynga时就深有体会。人们批评我说："和马克一起工作就像三年级踢足球，每周一他都兴奋不已地提出新点子。"他们说得没错。但或许我们可以通过构建这样的团队文化来改进："好吧，我们志向远大。我们如此雄心勃勃，以至于不愿满足于B+的成绩。即便能获得融资、取得些许进展，我们也要追随北极星般的目标，直到找到产品与市场的契合点。这次尝试不行，那就需要勇气。我们看看在座各位，有谁有足够的雄心去尝试？还是想离开加入已然势头强劲的公司？" 这对他们来说是合理的职业选择。但对我而言，真正的创业者模式就是要有勇气告诉团队和投资者："这次不行！"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly where I wanted to go, which is this other piece of advice you give, which is, "Kill hope before hope kills you." Talk about just what that is because so much of your advice is, "Kill your bad ideas quickly." So just talk about that and then I'm really curious to know what it takes to realize an idea is bad. When do you decide, "Okay, this is B+. Let's move on."
turns.zh: 这正是你想传达的核心观点："在希望将你吞噬之前，先斩断希望。" 能否具体解释一下这个理念？毕竟你的许多建议都是"迅速淘汰糟糕的想法"。请展开谈谈这个观点，同时我很想知道如何判断一个想法是否糟糕？何时会下定决心："好吧，这个只能打B+，继续前进吧。"

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: I don't know if I get credit for making up that quote, but I love it, kill hope before hope kills you. There's a difference between belief and hope. Hope is confidence without basis. Hope is just, it's a prayer, but it's not founded in anything that your lived experience. It's not founded in your experience with your product, your experience with people experiencing your product and the data. And I think that too many founders and teams keep going with the hope that this next release is going to do something magical. And I think that the best product makers, I like to say they're collecting winnings, they're not making bets. They already know. If you talk to Brian Chesky about his launches, he already knows that he has a hit. He's not launching it to find out if people like it. (00:34:52): And I talk about the difference between launching an MVP, a minimum viable product, and a maximum launchable product. Because if we're going off hope, we're getting to this MVP, minimum viable, that the viable is the word we got to kill along with hope because viable is where hope comes from. If it's viable, it might make it. And there's a difference between get in the market early, learn. You're putting a product out that you're going to learn from and you're putting a product out that you're going to launch that you think you believe, not hope, is going to be a hit. And it's really important to be crisp and to make that distinction. (00:35:38): And AI is a dangerous tool today. It's so powerful that it's dangerous. It's so powerful that it means we can get to a viable product in much less time and money than it took maybe three months instead of three years. And that's a dangerous drug because it means that... What I thought would happen where we'd be today is that people would be using AI to build these incredible testing machines, failure machines that are testing, I like to say more ideas in a week than your industry tests in a year. How are you testing a 100 ideas a day instead of one in three months? I think AI is being used more to build one idea in three months than a hundred ideas in a day. (00:36:25): And what would it look like? I like to say we should build it completely wrong before we know it's the right product. So build it wrong before you know it's right. And if you could build it right, great, but don't be slowed down by that. Because if we start off, if we say, "Okay, what can I believe today? I believe this is the wrong product." What are you going to do differently because you believe it's the wrong product? You are not going to waste three months building the wrong product. "Oh, I'd rather waste a day or a week building the wrong product. But the point of what I'm building is to learn. So is it good enough to get signal and to test my idea?" And I think we can usually pull that apart and test those pieces in the wrong way. It's so often it could be an ad. I cannot believe how many times a team hasn't even tested the ads for their product before they go and put in the markets an afterthought. (00:37:23): And it was so often at Zynga, it blew my mind. I mean, I'll give you one story from Zynga. When we were launching our first expansion pack for FarmVille, which these became massive business drivers for us, I think it was FarmVille English Countryside or something. The team came to me and they said, "Okay, we have a $10 million ad budget and we're going to start running ads before the launch." I'm like, "Wait, you have 25, 30 million people a day using your product, but you're going to put ads somewhere else for coming soon. You have these people engaged. What if you just put something on the game board? And what if you don't just start your product marketing, you're still doing product testing to see what gets the most heat? What if you start putting different art forms of your English Countryside locked on the game board and you just see how many clicks you get and you just start testing the look, the feel, the marketing message and at the same time when people click on it says, 'Coming soon, click here to be a pre-user, click here to get access two weeks before anybody else.'" (00:38:46): And it turned out everybody clicked on it because it's a change in your game board and it both gave us direction on what was the right marketing and the right variant of the product, but the unintended consequences was we started selling keys to people for you and a friend and we ended up selling $19 million worth of keys to get early access to the new expansion pack. And so we took something that was going to be afterthought advertising, try to drum up interest in this product and turn into something that gave us signal and direction on the product and revenues. And so often you can have, this is an existing product, but you could turn something that was going to be marketing into a kind of scarcity and heat-driving feature, something that could drive revenues or something else that matters. So the way we should be using AI is as a testing machine, a failure machine and a way to vibe code, Quadcode, but build the lowest possible cycled version of your product that you can get signal back on.
turns.zh:
我不知道这句话是否算是我原创的，但我很喜欢它——"在希望将你击垮之前，先将希望扼杀"。信念与希望之间存在着本质区别。希望是没有根基的自信，是祈祷而非基于经验的幻想。它不基于你对产品的实际体验，也不基于用户对产品的反馈，更不基于数据分析。我发现太多创业者和团队总怀着"下一版产品能创造奇迹"的幻想。优秀的产品经理更像是在"收割胜利果实”，而非孤注一掷。他们早已心知肚明。谈到Brian Chesky的发布策略，他早在产品上线前就确信产品会成功——他不会用发布来验证市场反应。  

我区分了MVP（最小可行产品）与最大化可行产品的差异。若依赖希望，MVP只是个最低可行产品，因为"可行性"本身就是希望的源泉。若产品可行，它才有机会成功。但早期市场验证与赌博有本质区别：前者是试错迭代，后者是盲目押注。  

当下AI技术堪称双刃剑。其强大功能让我们能以极低成本快速验证产品，但也催生了危险的副作用——用AI快速生成大量测试样本，却忽视了行业多年积累的经验。  

我主张先构建错误产品，再逐步优化。若你坚信某个产品方向错误，何不尽快调整？若你坚持正确路径，也不必为此拖延。关键在于先行动，再反思。  

我举例说明AI如何用于验证假设：比如测试100个创意比测试3个月才得出结论更高效。  

最后，关于广告策略：团队常在产品发布前匆忙投放广告，却忽视基础优化。Zynga的案例令人震惊——《FarmVille》首次扩展包发布前，他们预留1000万美元广告预算，却未进行有效测试。
这些用户已经被充分调动起来了。要是你在游戏界面上放点东西试试呢？如果你不急着开展产品营销，而是继续进行产品测试，看看哪些元素最能引发关注呢？比如在游戏界面上展示不同风格的英伦乡村艺术品，看看能获得多少点击量。同时，在用户点击后跳转到“即将上线”页面，引导他们成为预览用户，或者提前两周获取访问权限。

（00:38:46）结果所有人都点击了这个界面。这不仅为我们指明了正确的营销方向和产品优化路径，更带来了意外收获——我们开始向用户出售“你和朋友的专属密钥”，最终售出价值1900万美元的密钥，让用户提前体验新扩展包。原本只是作为辅助宣传的举措，却意外转化为产品反馈机制和创收利器。

即便面对现有产品，我们也能将营销手段转化为稀缺感制造器、话题引爆器。通过AI赋能的测试引擎、失败引擎和代码共振机制（Quadcode），快速构建最小可行产品版本，快速获取用户反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to ask about something that I think might be on people's minds as they hear you talk. For a lot of product builders, when I think Zynga, they're not like, "This is the product I want to build." And there's a spectrum of products you guys have built. There's like FarmVille and CityVille and all these things that I think turn some people off. And then there's like Poker, Words with Friends, Mafia Wars that I think people are like, "Oh, that's amazing. I love that." Can you just speak to that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想问一下，我觉得当人们听你讲话时，他们可能会想到一些问题。对于很多产品开发者来说，比如说想到Zynga时，他们不会想“这就是我想开发的产品”。你们开发的产品种类繁多，有《农场小镇》《城市小镇》之类的，这些游戏可能让一些人望而却步。但也有《扑克牌》《拼字游戏》《黑手党战争》之类的，我觉得人们会觉得“哦，太棒了，我超爱这款游戏”。你能谈谈这方面的看法吗？

turns.speaker: Mark Pincus
turns.en: Sure. I think if I'm unpacking that when you say that the products turn people off, it's funny you say that because FarmVille and CityVille were our biggest hits in terms of installs, engagement, retention, revenues. Now, Words with Friends and Poker were more enduring because they made the transition to mobile and the other games didn't. There's a whole other story, but I think the part you're getting to is that Zynga was in a lot of ways a victim of its own success, that our games were so viral and took over the feeds on Facebook so much that your friend who was playing it started to bug you as a person not playing it and that's fair. (00:41:31): But what I would say, I think what's misunderstood about Zynga from the beginning and why we succeeded and we created eight massive hits out of 10 mass large game launches. We had a very high hit rate. It wasn't that we were good at virality. It was that we were focused on two things that I think we did better than anybody else and we had lots of competitors, lots and copying and we still managed to keep winning. And so it couldn't be that we were just spammier or better at virality. First, we had this core mission and focus around connecting the world through games and Bing Gordon and I kept coming back to this idea that I love and I want your founders, product makers watching this to join me in thinking about, which is how can we add more dimensionality? I love this idea of, it's why I call it bold beat. It's how do I take this thing that's kind of gotten boring and wrote, poker or whatever, how do I add a whole new dimension to it? (00:42:42): And by adding social, by adding real identities, by giving you this, you're doing social networking, you're in this cocktail party and now we're giving you a way to actually meet new people or improve your relationships in a game. Well, the reason why people, so many, especially middle-aged women love FarmVille and these games was because they had this hobby, but they weren't doing it alone and they were doing it with their good friends, making new friends. And in the game, our most successful features were co-op play. There were things that let you do gifting and do things of value for your friends. And so we called the games invest, express and connect. You could do something that was, you were being seen as creative. I like to say people don't want to be creative, they want to feel creative. So we were letting you feel creative, look creative to people. (00:43:45): It's what Midjourney does for me today. And then we were letting you... So you were expressing yourself and then you were connecting with people around it. So that was the first thing. And then if you think at a mechanical metric level, our core metric was retention, not virality. We grew, we outlasted everybody because we had the best retention. I think we were the only consumer company in the world that tracked Day 365 retention. I don't think anyone tracks it today. I talk about in the book, I think it's a gift to your founders. I believe that the most valuable companies in the world, well, statistically this is true, they have the highest Day 365 retention. Can you build against Day 365 retention? Yes. We can't wait till Day 365. We can find early indicators of a positive Day 365 and a negative Day 365 retention. (00:44:44): If you have low D1, low D30, you will probably not have high Day 365. So those track, those are correlated, but you can have the opposite. You can have very high Day 30 and a zero Day 365, which is most products. And if you don't think about why someone would use this in a year, if you don't have that mentality, it turns out when someone tries our product, they think that way too. They kind of think, "Is this worth investing in?" Whether it's a game or a camera, it's, "Am I going to use this in a year? Should I tell my friends about this or should I bother investing? Should I bother giving it information about me or whatever?" And I think there's a mentality to that. (00:45:32): And I like to say viral-based companies, and there's been many, be real. We've seen these, they're sinking speedboats. They're trying to drive faster than they're sinking. They're trying to get more people in. You can either go faster, bail water out faster, which is trying to get people back or plug the hole in the boat or build a better boat that doesn't have a hole. But we were tracking both in our games, in our network, what was the retention? And we were really constantly thinking about that. And I think the two things to take away from Zynga's success in my opinion that I hold is to have a strong innovation vision that translates to what your teams are doing every week. And we even built a metric that's still not used by anyone. This is an Easter egg if this doesn't get cut and anyone's still listening, we built a metric called ASN and it stood for, we measured what was your active social network. (00:46:44): So we looked at how many round trips you had with a friend or another player, meaning you took a turn and they took a turn back, you gifted them and they gifted you back. And we found that if you went from zero ASN to one, there was an 80% chance we saw you again in the next month. And if we got you to a four, there was an 80% chance we'd see you 22 out of the next 30 days. And so we could actually build and innovate against that metric and it made sense because if you saw positive feedback loops, it's like someone likes your photos, comments, that's probably the biggest dopamine hit we get.

好的。我觉得你说产品让人们失去兴趣，这挺有趣的，因为《农场主》和《城市城堡》曾是我们在安装量、用户参与度、留存率和营收方面最成功的游戏。现在《朋友圈拼字游戏》和《扑克王》更经久不衰，因为它们成功转型为移动端游戏，而其他游戏却没能做到。这背后还有更深层的原因，但我认为你想说的是Zynga在某种程度上成了自身成功的受害者——我们的游戏太容易传播，在Facebook动态消息中占据大量空间，以至于玩这款游戏的朋友会烦到不玩的人，这很正常。（00:41:31）但我想说的是，人们从一开始就误解了Zynga的成功之道，以及我们为何能从10款大型游戏中打造出8款爆款。我们成功率极高，不是因为擅长病毒式传播，而是因为专注于两件事——这两点远超其他竞争对手。尽管面临众多模仿者，我们始终能保持领先。首先，我们坚守连接全球玩家的核心使命。宾·戈登和我反复思考一个理念：如何为游戏增添更多维度？我称之为"大胆突破"——如何为已然乏味的游戏注入新活力？（00:42:42）通过社交化和真实身份认证，让玩家在游戏中建立社交关系——比如在鸡尾酒会上结交新朋友，或深化现有关系。这正是《农场主》等游戏深受中年女性喜爱的原因——她们既能享受爱好，也能与好友互动。游戏中最成功的功能是合作玩法，比如赠送礼物和为朋友创造价值。我们将游戏核心价值定义为"投资、表达和连接"，让玩家展现创造力，同时在他人眼中变得富有创造力。（00:43:45）这正是Midjourney如今为我带来的体验。接着，我们赋予玩家自我表达和社交互动的能力。这就是第一步。从数据层面看，我们关注的核心指标是留存率，而非病毒式传播。我们通过卓越的留存率脱颖而出，是全球唯一追踪365天留存率的消费品公司。如今没人再追踪这个数据了。我在书中提到，这是给创业者的宝贵启示。统计数据显示，全球最具价值的公司往往拥有最高的365天留存率。如何优化365天留存率？答案是提前预警。（00:44:44）低D1（第一天留存率）、低D30（第三十天留存率）往往意味着低365天留存率。因此这些数据相关，但反向关联同样存在——可能D30高但365天归零（多数产品如此）。如果你不思考用户为何会离开，
用一年时间去验证，如果你没有这种心态，结果就是当人们试用我们的产品时，他们也会抱着同样的疑问。他们会想：“这东西值得投资吗？” 无论是游戏还是相机，他们都会思考：“我一年后还会用吗？我该不该把这个推荐给朋友？值得投入精力吗？我该不该分享自己的信息之类的？” 我觉得这背后有一种思维定式。  
（00:45:32）：我常说那些基于病毒式传播的公司（有很多这样的例子），必须保持真实。我们见过太多这种情况——它们就像正在下沉的快艇。它们试图开得比下沉速度更快，拼命吸纳用户。要么加速前进，快速排出积水（比如留住老用户），要么堵住船体漏洞，要么造一艘没有漏洞的新船。但我们在游戏和社交网络中始终关注用户留存率，并持续为此优化策略。在我看来，Zynga成功的两大秘诀在于：制定能转化为团队每周实际行动的创新愿景。我们甚至开发了一项至今仍未被广泛应用的指标——这算是个彩蛋，如果没被剪掉且有人在听的话。我们创建了一个名为ASN的指标，代表“活跃社交网络”（active social network）。  
（00:46:44）：我们监测用户与好友或其他玩家的互动频率——你先行动对方反馈，再由对方回应。研究发现，如果ASN从0提升到1，次月复访概率达80%；若提升至4，未来30天内复访概率则达80%。基于此指标进行优化非常有效，因为正向反馈循环（比如别人点赞你的照片、评论等）能带来最强烈的多巴胺刺激。

……这是网络上最热门的十大活动之一。我觉得存在潜在需求。我热爱游戏，也喜欢和家人一起玩，但很难找到一起玩的人，而且投入成本太高了。简直是费尽周折才能让别人和你一起玩游戏。（00:50:19）：我让我的侄子们——他们都是游戏狂热爱好者——和我一起玩《国家崛起》。我们为他们准备了两台电脑，为我自己也准备了两台。其中一台电脑开着FaceTime视频通话，同时游戏也在运行，所有人都连接到游戏服务器上。我们只玩了一次。我当时就想：“这也太麻烦了。” 虽然玩得很开心，但只玩了一次。我的想法是：“好吧，我相信这应该能成为大众市场活动。我相信成年人想给自己一个玩游戏的许可，但必须让它足够容易上手，成本也不能太高。”（00:51:05）：免费的，不是那种普通的免费活动——那种活动要60美元购买游戏。所以我把它做成免费的，并说：“我要用大家熟悉的游戏。三次点击就能进入，参与时间5到15分钟，你肯定会爱上它。这就像面包屑一样自然。假设我们不去漫画书店，但如果漫画出现在报纸上，人们也会去读。”所以我相信存在潜在需求。事实上，如今游戏行业规模达2800亿美元。我确实认为还有未被开发的巨大增长空间，因为游戏行业规模巨大，但参与度却很低，成年人基本不参与，或者只有少数人在玩。规模巨大，但我认识的人里没几个玩的。好吧，所以社交和消费领域。我相信我们对社交需求远超表面需求，我们一直在网上社交。（00:52:13）：我们用Snapchat、Instagram和TikTok，但我觉得它们失去了激情。我总在思考激情问题。人们登录Instagram时还有热情吗？还是感觉像吃薯片一样？这些是正能量还是负能量？我觉得有个有趣的点，查看NPS（净推荐值）数据发现，当人们退出Facebook和Instagram后，NPS从正35降到负35。（00:52:56）：人们有种戒烟后的感觉。他们会自豪地说不玩Instagram了。他们觉得自己没错过派对。就像“哇，我戒掉了。” 所以我想说，这是互联网上最大的未开发机会。我坚信会有人为AI时代重塑社交体验，但他们该怎么做呢？（00:53:28）：我猜他们会重新赋予我们生产力……我们得到的部分，人们忘记Facebook曾为我们带来巨大的社交生产力。我们能和300个或1000个朋友保持联系。LinkedIn至今仍能提供生产力，但后来偏离了这条路线，走向浪费时间的方向，因为他们想增加互动和广告，减少LinkedIn内容，但Instagram现在可能受TikTok启发，开始这么做了。（00:54:08）：所以我认为在社交体验中可以实现新一级生产力提升，让我们的代理能让我们更紧密地与关心的人保持联系，同时不浪费时间。我还要说，有个侧面问题……
嗯，我把这种社交活动叫做"鸡尾酒会"。好吧。这对我来说是一个重要的本能直觉。当我想到鸡尾酒会时，我会想它到底在哪里举行，或者应该在哪里举行，又该如何为它增添趣味？（00:54:49）：我们都乐于举办鸡尾酒会，即便不是主办方，也乐于参与其中。当我们看到一场精彩的鸡尾酒会时，自然能感知到它的魅力——那种身处其中的愉悦感，让人不禁感叹"真高兴能来这里"。它从单纯的社交义务（比如参加生日派对）转变为一种享受，人们会沉浸其中，甚至会产生贪恋之情——"我太爱这个派对了！我喜欢在这里结识的新朋友！"而一场成功的鸡尾酒会能带来什么？往往能收获优质的人脉资源。（00:55:13）：对我而言，鸡尾酒会的起点是Napster时代，当时我们突然能彼此互联，获取音乐文件就是优质的人脉资源。之后Friendster、Facebook、LinkedIn的出现则提升了人脉拓展的效率。相比之下，过去我们要么在Google上搜索线索，要么浏览Craigslist，那些平台充斥着大量无用信息。而现在人们会感叹："天哪，我在Friendster上找到了约会对象，这真是高质量的人脉资源啊！我和Friendster上的对象约会非常愉快。"（00:55:49）：所以我想告诉大家，如果想重塑社交模式，就要寻找那种"鸡尾酒会"的场景——或者亲自举办，然后思考如何实现高效的人脉拓展。说到"人脉拓展"可能听起来有些生硬，但LinkedIn不就是从这里起步的吗？其核心价值在于提供实用工具，让人们在社交场合中拓展人脉。如今以Zynga为例，我曾设想："我要把游戏引入社交平台，让用户在游戏中拓展社交维度，因为他们本来就热衷于Facebook。我要为他们创造更多互动机会。"（00:56:32）：如今我们都在手机或GPT上消磨时间，但社交平台却缺乏那种活力四射的社交场面。我的灵感来自于网络早期那种安静、孤独的社交场景。我想向听众发起挑战：如何让社交场景重新热闹起来，如何让鸡尾酒会既社交又高效，相信你们一定能从中挖掘到宝藏。我想回归到你们的问题核心——如何判断一个创意是否达到B+级？对吧？

(01:00:21): So we're getting more and more metaverse in. It's not being in this other escape to immersive world.
